proofParity: eth_getProof byte sizes are near-identical across clients at every milestone — 3.5× p50 8,071 B (NM) vs 8,072 B (Geth); 5× mean ~11.4 KB on both — exactly as expected for the same state root. EIP-1186 proofs are client-agnostic, so witness size is comparable regardless of which client serves it.
summary: At the two work-matched milestones (3.5× and 5×) the clients land at opposite optima: Geth serves reads with a several-× lower tail (3.5×: p99 22 ms vs 160 ms; 5×: 110 ms vs 360 ms) on ~2.4–3× lighter memory, while Nethermind pushes ~2.5–3× the gas throughput and keeps a smaller DB. The 7× and 10× runs (pinned-window, but NOT work-matched — read the per-milestone warning on the chart) confirm both clients execute the full state through 10× without collapse and with 0 RPC failures; Geth stays 4–5× lighter on RAM there, and at 10× the on-disk DB flips (Geth 3.35 vs NM 4.22 TB). The 10× read-latency looks reversed (NM 2 ms vs Geth 13 ms) only because the 10× payload stream is light, leaving NM idle capacity to serve reads.
workMatched: One caveat colours the read-latency numbers: latency is coupled to import duty cycle. At 3.5× the latency shown is the 60-minute run; at 5× it's the 5-minute run, because the 5× 60-minute run was NOT work-matched — Geth imported ~1,300 blocks vs Nethermind's ~560 (≈2.3× the work, and far heavier blocks by the end), which pushed Geth's 60-minute read tail to ~520 ms while Nethermind (throttled by memory pressure) sat at ~180 ms. A cleaner 60-minute Geth re-run reproduced this exactly — 1,301 blocks, aggregate p99 520 ms, RSS flat at ~42 GB as GC keeps pace. At the equal-work 5-minute mark Geth's tail (~110 ms) was well below Nethermind's (~360 ms). The honest cross-client statement is per unit of work: Geth stays the lighter, lower-tail reader; Nethermind the higher-throughput executor. A block-count-capped run is the open item that fully decouples the two.
caveat: Gas/s is not a strict like-for-like statistic — Geth reports a decaying go-metrics timer, Nethermind a gauge — treat it directionally. The read window (recent_block_window=8–64) sits inside both clients' served-state window.
